title: Knots And Covering Spaces
notes: Open with the chapter question: what data survives when a closed curve in three-space is redrawn? The 3D trefoil is the object; the planar diagram is a controlled loss of depth. Preview the route from local crossings to global invariants and say that the lecture follows the notebook artifacts rather than a generic knot-theory survey.

title: A Projection Loses Depth
notes: Use the trefoil projection as a diagnostic rather than a decorative picture. The projection direction forgets one coordinate, and the three transverse collisions become useful only because the missing depth coordinate tells which strand passes over. The minimum depth gap is a numerical sanity check that the diagram is not hiding a tangency.

title: Diagram Data Is Local
notes: Slow down on the distinction between a knot and a diagram. A diagram is an annotated immersion of a circle in the plane, with finitely many local over-under decisions. Students should inspect how each crossing contributes a tiny piece of data while the ambient isotopy class lives in three dimensions.

title: Reidemeister Moves
notes: Present the three moves as the legal edit operations for diagrams of the same knot. The outside of the small disk is fixed, so all action is local. The point is not to memorize drawings, but to recognize that curl, cancellation, and slide changes are harmless at the level of ambient isotopy.

title: Invariance Means A Ledger
notes: Connect Reidemeister moves to invariants by asking what a proposed calculation must survive. Crossing number alone is suspicious because a type one move can change it. The ledger format makes students check whether a quantity is diagram data, projection data, or actual knot data before trusting it.

title: Wirtinger Relations
notes: Introduce Wirtinger presentations as a local-to-global conversion. Each overpass contributes a generator in the complement, and each crossing records how an underpass loop changes when it passes under an overpass. The graph artifact is a proof scaffold: generators feed relations, and relations assemble into the knot group.

title: Trefoil Group Test
notes: The trefoil relation aba equals bab is useful because it has a small nonabelian witness. Sending a and b to two transpositions in S3 satisfies the relation but the images do not commute. That finite quotient separates the trefoil group from the infinite cyclic group of the unknot without solving the whole group.

title: Seifert Surface Model
notes: Now move from the complement to a spanning surface. The Seifert construction smooths crossings according to orientation, fills the resulting circles by disks, and reinstalls crossings as twisted bands. The band model keeps the surface orientable while showing where the genus is forced by the original three crossings.

title: Genus From Bookkeeping
notes: Make the Euler characteristic calculation explicit and mechanical. For the trefoil model, two Seifert circles and three bands give chi equal to minus one. With one boundary component, the equation chi equals two minus two g minus b gives genus one. This is a surface invariant extracted from diagram bookkeeping.

title: Covering Maps
notes: Shift vocabulary from knots to covering spaces. A covering map looks locally like identical sheets over each small base neighborhood, even though loops can permute sheets globally. This prepares the bridge to knot groups: fundamental group elements act by lifting paths and watching where endpoints land.

title: Lifts And Deck Shifts
notes: Use the circle cover as the cleanest endpoint-motion model. A loop of winding number one lifts from a chosen starting point to the next integer translate. Deck transformations preserve the covering map, so on the real line they are exactly integer translations. This is the prototype for the deck-shift variable t.

title: Deck Transformations
notes: The finite graph cover is intentionally not regular. It has four sheets over the base wedge, but only two deck transformations commute with both monodromy permutations. Ask students to compare sheet count with deck transformation count; equality is a special regular-cover behavior, not part of the definition of covering map.

title: Infinite Cyclic Cover
notes: Tie the covering-space language back to knots. Abelianizing a knot group sends every meridian to one generator of Z, producing an infinite cyclic cover of the complement. The deck group is Z, and one chosen deck shift is recorded algebraically as multiplication by t in the Alexander module.

title: Alexander Matrix
notes: Explain the matrix as relations after the deck shift has been remembered. The trefoil presentation matrix has entries in the Laurent polynomial ring, so row and column operations carry unit ambiguities. The determinant t squared minus t plus one is the trefoil Alexander polynomial up to multiplication by plus or minus a power of t.

title: Polynomial As A Diagnostic
notes: Use the unit-circle plot and edit lab to make the polynomial tangible. The true trefoil row has determinant t squared minus t plus one, value one at t equals one, and zero symmetry residual. The edited row deliberately breaks the crossing record, showing how sensitive the determinant is to matrix data.

title: Chapter Synthesis
notes: Close by tracing the same object through the chapter pipeline. A knot gives a diagram; a diagram gives crossing relations; the complement group controls covers; deck shifts turn into algebra; the Alexander polynomial becomes a compact invariant. The final exercise asks students to name which parts are local choices and which are invariant.
